title: Density Histograms Across Dictionary Sizes
takeaway: Across five sparsity settings, each panel overlays the feature-density histograms of six autoencoders whose dictionaries run from 512 up to 131,072 units. Widening the dictionary does not just yield more features: it keeps pushing the left edge of the distribution further left, so rarer features keep appearing. The paper reads this as a sign that no dictionary size tried so far has exhausted the one-layer transformer's features, and states it as a suggestion rather than a result.
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Five panels, one per setting of the weight on the sparsity penalty — the [[l1-coefficient]] $\lambda$, printed in each panel's corner as `L1=`, running 0.001, 0.004, 0.006, 0.008 and 0.01.

Inside each panel sit six curves. Each curve is one trained [[sparse-autoencoder]], and the legend value "N Learned Sparse" gives its dictionary width: 512, 4096, 16384, 32768, 65536 or 131072 hidden units. The transformer's MLP has 512 neurons, so those widths span 1× to 256× ([[expansion-factor]]). All runs shown are on the "A" transformer.

### How to read one curve

Each curve is a [[feature-density-histogram]]. The x axis is $\log_{10}$ of a feature's [[feature-density]] — the fraction of training tokens on which its activation is nonzero. A feature at $-4$ fires on one token in ten thousand; one at $-7$ fires on one in ten million.

The y axis is a raw count of features per density bin. It is not normalised by dictionary size. A wider run therefore starts with an advantage, since more units means more counts, so height alone is not the evidence.

### What each panel shows

The broad right-hand mode is the [[high-density-cluster]], whose features the paper reports are almost all interpretable. The narrow spikes jammed against the left edge near $10^{-7}$ are the [[ultralow-density-cluster]]: almost none are interpretable, and the paper treats them as an artifact of autoencoder training rather than a property of the transformer — [[dead-neurons]] in all but name.

Raising $\lambda$ shifts everything left. At $\lambda=0.001$ the bulk sits near $10^{-4}$ and a second bump sits right of $10^{-2}$; those are features firing on more than 1% of tokens, which the paper's own checklist reads as the penalty being too weak ([[feature-density-diagnostics]]). By $\lambda=0.01$ nothing survives above $10^{-2}$.

### The argument

Within a panel, read the curves in order of width. Two things happen at once, and the second carries the claim.

The curves get taller, which is just more features. And their left edge keeps sliding left, which means the rarest feature recovered keeps getting rarer.

Were the 512-neuron layer's [[true-features]] exhausted, extra capacity should go dead or produce duplicates. Instead new mass appears in the rare tail at every size tried. The caption says "suggesting", and the hedge is earned: the plot counts features and cannot separate a genuinely new one from [[feature-splitting]] of an existing one. The paper also warns that at large width and large $\lambda$ the two density clusters overlap, so the tall spikes in the $\lambda=0.008$ and $\lambda=0.01$ panels should not be read as all real features.

terms.definition: The quantity every panel histograms: for one feature, the fraction of tokens in the training set on which that feature's activation is nonzero. It is the paper's cheap proxy for how well an autoencoder run is doing.
The base-10 logarithm of that fraction, used because densities span many orders of magnitude. A value of -5 means the feature fires on one token in 100,000.
The number of autoencoder features whose density falls in a given histogram bin. It is an absolute count, not a share of the dictionary, so curves for larger dictionaries sit higher by construction.
The number of hidden units in the sparse autoencoder, i.e. how many dictionary directions it can learn. The paper uses it interchangeably with autoencoder size or dictionary width.
The dictionary with exactly as many units as the transformer's MLP has neurons, run A/0. It is not overcomplete, and its curve is the lowest and shortest-tailed in every panel.
The 8x dictionary, run A/1, which is the run most of the paper's individual feature analysis uses. Here it is one of the smaller curves.
A 32x dictionary. Its curve sits between the small and large runs in both height and leftward reach.
A 64x dictionary, one step up the size ladder.
A 128x dictionary, second largest in the sweep.
The largest dictionary in the paper, 256x the MLP width. Its curve is the tallest in every panel and reaches furthest into the rare tail, which is the figure's main evidence.

The coefficient multiplying the L1 penalty on the autoencoder's hidden activations in its training loss. Each panel holds it fixed while varying dictionary size, so the six curves in a panel are comparable.

One hidden unit of the trained autoencoder, understood as a direction in MLP activation space that fires on some interpretable condition. Each feature contributes exactly one entry to one histogram bin.

The left mode, the narrow spikes near 10^-7, made of units that fire on fewer than roughly one token in a million. The paper says almost none are interpretable and treats them as a training artifact, not as features of the transformer.
The broad right mode of each curve, which the paper says is anecdotally almost all interpretable, even though its absolute densities are still tiny.

Autoencoder hidden units with zero activation across a large number of datapoints. Training resamples them, but ultralow-density units that fire just barely enough to escape the check remain effectively dead.

All dictionaries plotted here were trained on the MLP activations of the paper's main one-layer transformer, called A. A second transformer B, differing only in initialization seed, is used elsewhere for universality checks.
Dictionary width divided by the 512 MLP neurons: how many times more feature directions than neurons the autoencoder has. The legend values correspond to 1x, 8x, 32x, 64x, 128x and 256x.
The features the transformer actually uses, as opposed to the ones a particular dictionary happens to learn. The figure's claim is about whether the dictionaries have covered them yet.

The observation that widening the dictionary makes a single feature divide into a family of more specific ones covering roughly the same territory. It is the main reason more curve mass does not automatically mean genuinely new features.

numbers.meaning: The six dictionary widths overlaid in every panel, as given in the legend. They form the sequence of runs the paper calls A/0 through A/5, trained with matched settings so that size is the only variable within a panel.
Also the width of the transformer's MLP layer. The smallest dictionary equals it exactly, so that run is not overcomplete and can at best relabel the neuron basis.
The same six widths expressed as multiples of 512. The paper's headline sweep runs from 1x up to 256x, and most of its individual feature work is at the 8x run.

The five L1 coefficients, one per panel. They are shown because the sparsity penalty and the dictionary width interact: raising the penalty makes each feature fire on fewer tokens and shifts every curve left.
Densities from one token in ten million up to one in ten. The right end only has occupants at low L1, where the penalty is weak enough to leave some features firing very often.
At the two strongest penalties nothing is left above 1% density, so the axis simply stops earlier. The distributions have been pushed entirely into the rare region.
One token in ten million: the density at which the ultralow spikes sit, and roughly the resolution floor of the measurement. The paper reads features here as almost never interpretable.
One token in ten thousand: roughly where the high density cluster peaks in the weakest-penalty panel. Even this, the paper notes, is a very low absolute rate.

The diagnostic threshold from the paper's hyperparameter checklist. A substantial number of features above 1% density is taken to mean the L1 coefficient is too low, which is visible as the secondary bump right of -2 in the L1 = 0.001 panel.
The tallest bin in that panel, on the 131,072-unit curve near a density of 10^-4.4. It is around 2.6% of that dictionary's units landing in a single bin.
The tallest bin at the second penalty setting, again on the largest dictionary, with the mode having shifted slightly left compared to L1 = 0.001.

A spike at the extreme left edge, near 10^-7, on the 131,072-unit curve. Unlike the other panel maxima this one is ultralow density cluster mass, not interpretable features, and a second spike of roughly 3,900 sits just to its right.

A tall narrow pile-up near 10^-5.6 on the largest dictionary. The paper cautions that at large width and large L1 the ultralow and high density clusters overlap, so density alone cannot say how much of this spike is real features.
The largest count anywhere in the figure, near 10^-5.7 on the 131,072-unit curve, with the corresponding 65,536-unit peak around 4,500. The same overlap caveat applies.

The number of MLP activation vectors the autoencoders are trained on. Feature density is a fraction of tokens in this training set, so it is measured over a very large sample, which is what makes densities as low as 10^-7 meaningful at all.
The number of Pile tokens the one-layer transformer itself was trained on. The paper overtrains it deliberately, hoping this yields cleaner representations in superposition.
